prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "BeOne Medicines Ltd." (ticker ONC), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ONC", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: BeOne Medicines Ltd.
markets: BTK inhibitors for B-cell blood cancers (CLL, MCL, WM, MZL, FL)
PD-1 immuno-oncology (solid tumours, esp. gastric, esophageal, lung)
China oncology and in-licensed specialty drugs (Amgen products)

mission.plain: Discover and develop new cancer medicines quickly and make them more affordable and accessible to patients around the world.

about.plain: BeOne (formerly BeiGene) invents and sells medicines that fight cancer, especially blood cancers. Its biggest product is a pill called BRUKINSA that blocks a protein cancer cells need to grow. It runs its own huge network of doctors and hospitals that test new drugs, which lets it test medicines faster and cheaper than many rivals. It was started in Beijing in 2010 and is now based in Basel, Switzerland, with most of its sales in the United States.
about.customers: Hospitals, cancer clinics, specialty pharmacies and drug wholesalers, paid for mostly by insurers and government health systems.
about.everyday: If a grandparent is treated for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (a common blood cancer in older adults), the daily pill they take may well be BRUKINSA.

money.plain: zanubrutinib, a BTK inhibitor for CLL and lymphomas ($3.9B in FY2025, company-rounded)
tislelizumab, a PD-1 antibody for stomach, esophageal and lung cancers ($737M)
XGEVA, BLINCYTO and KYPROLIS under license ($486M)
smaller in-licensed drugs, biosimilars and partner royalties/fees
BCL2 inhibitor; FDA accelerated approval in relapsed mantle cell lymphoma in 2026, aiming to pair with BRUKINSA as fixed-duration therapy
tacabrutideg (BGB-16673) BTK degrader and CDK4 inhibitor BGB-43395 in Phase 3 breast cancer

result.summary: BeOne has a real and growing moat in B-cell blood cancers: BRUKINSA beat AbbVie/J&J's Imbruvica head-to-head (ALPINE trial) and became the global BTK-class leader, with 77 market approvals and $3.9B of FY2025 sales. Its in-house global clinical machine (about 3,800 clinical staff, CRO-light) gives it a speed and cost edge that is hard to copy. The advantage is concentrated in one product, though, and patents, newer BTK agents (Lilly's Jaypirca) and fixed-duration regimens could erode it later in the decade.

pricingPower.evidence: BRUKINSA holds premium US list pricing comparable to Imbruvica and Calquence while US sales grew 45% in FY2025 to $2.8B, and GAAP gross margin rose to 87.3% from 84.3%; but in China TEVIMBRA and other drugs required steep price cuts for National Reimbursement Drug List inclusion, and PD-1s are a crowded, price-competitive class.

moats.evidence: BRUKINSA's patents and its superior head-to-head ALPINE data versus ibrutinib (better progression-free survival, fewer cardiac events) give it a strong clinical reputation among hematologists; the corporate brand is little known to the public.
Continuous BTK therapy means patients stay on a tolerated drug for years, and physicians rarely switch a responding CLL patient; but new patients can be started on rivals freely.
Drug value does not rise with the number of users.
Internal clinical operations across 40+ markets and China-based R&D let BeOne run large Phase 3 programs at lower cost per patient than many Western peers; scale is still smaller than big pharma's.
The BTK class supports several large players (Imbruvica, Calquence, BRUKINSA, Jaypirca), so the niche is not naturally limited to one supplier.

Its founding model of doing drug development in-house globally, with China speed and cost, contrasts with big pharma's outsourced CRO model, which incumbents cannot easily replicate without restructuring.

A ~3,800-person global clinical team and 40+ Phase 3 or potentially registrational trials allow fast enrolment and execution, evidenced by taking BRUKINSA, TEVIMBRA and sonrotoclax from discovery to approvals in-house.
Owns global rights to BRUKINSA, TEVIMBRA (after Novartis returned rights in 2023), sonrotoclax and the BGB-16673 BTK degrader, a hematology franchise few rivals hold in one company.

customers.evidence: CEO John Oyler says BRUKINSA has 'firmly established itself as the global leader in the BTK inhibitor class', with global sales up 49% in FY2025 and long-term CLL efficacy and safety data driving physician adoption; patients on continuous therapy tend to stay on it for years.

talent.evidence: Nearly 12,000 employees and 1,200+ research scientists; it has recruited senior big-pharma leaders and benefits from China's large scientist pool, but it does not appear on widely cited best-employer rankings and faced geopolitical scrutiny (e.g. BIOSECURE Act debates).

product.evidence: BRUKINSA is the only BTK inhibitor to show superior progression-free survival head-to-head against ibrutinib (ALPINE, NEJM 2022/2023) and is approved in 77 markets; TEVIMBRA is approved in the US, EU, China and Japan but is one of many PD-1s.

competitors.name: AstraZeneca
competitors.note: Calquence (acalabrutinib) is BRUKINSA's most direct BTK rival; also Imfinzi in PD-(L)1 and fixed-duration CLL combinations.

competitors.name: AbbVie
competitors.note: Imbruvica (ibrutinib, US) in BTK and Venclexta (venetoclax) versus sonrotoclax in BCL2.

competitors.name: Johnson & Johnson
competitors.note: Imbruvica outside the US; Darzalex and other hematology drugs.

competitors.name: Eli Lilly
competitors.note: Jaypirca (pirtobrutinib), a non-covalent BTK inhibitor expanding into earlier-line CLL.

competitors.name: Roche
competitors.note: Venclexta partner with AbbVie, Gazyva, Columvi/Lunsumio bispecifics in lymphoma, and Tecentriq in PD-L1.

competitors.name: Merck & Co.
competitors.note: Keytruda, the dominant PD-1, competes with TEVIMBRA in gastric, esophageal and lung cancers.

competitors.name: Bristol Myers Squibb
competitors.note: Opdivo in PD-1; Breyanzi CAR-T in CLL and lymphoma.

competitors.name: Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals
competitors.note: Camrelizumab PD-1 and broad oncology portfolio in China.

competitors.name: Akeso
competitors.note: Ivonescimab (PD-1/VEGF) and penpulimab threaten PD-1 monotherapy in China and globally (with Summit Therapeutics).

competitors.name: Shanghai Junshi Biosciences
competitors.note: Toripalimab PD-1 in China and the US.

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Kisqali in HR+ breast cancer, where BeOne's CDK4 inhibitor is in Phase 3; former TEVIMBRA partner.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Ibrance and a next-generation CDK4 inhibitor in breast cancer.

marketShare.market: Global BTK inhibitor sales (BRUKINSA, Imbruvica, Calquence only; Jaypirca and China-only BTKs excluded; approximate, from company-reported product sales)

threats: Heavy concentration: BRUKINSA was about 73% of FY2025 revenue, so any safety, patent or pricing hit is material.
Fixed-duration CLL regimens (venetoclax-based, and AstraZeneca's acalabrutinib-venetoclax) could shrink years of continuous BTK therapy per patient.
Lilly's non-covalent Jaypirca moving into earlier-line CLL, plus BTK degraders from rivals.
US drug pricing reform (IRA Medicare negotiation, most-favoured-nation pricing pressure) and eventual BRUKINSA patent expiry in the 2030s.
US-China geopolitical risk (BIOSECURE-type legislation, tariffs) given large R&D and manufacturing footprint in China.
Crowded PD-1 market where TEVIMBRA competes with Keytruda, Opdivo and PD-1/VEGF bispecifics like ivonescimab.

ceo.name: John V. Oyler
ceo.background: Co-founder (with scientist Xiaodong Wang); MIT bachelor's degree, Stanford MBA; earlier McKinsey consultant and founder/CEO of Galenea and BioDuro.

c1.evidence: BRUKINSA is now the global BTK-inhibitor class leader ($3.9B FY2025 sales, up 49%), but BTK inhibitors are a maturing, not emerging, industry within oncology.

c2.evidence: Physicians choose BRUKINSA for its superior head-to-head ALPINE results and cleaner cardiac safety versus ibrutinib, an evidence-based edge backed by patents that should last into the 2030s.

c3.evidence: BeOne is known to oncologists but not to ordinary people, and it renamed itself from BeiGene in 2025, so it lacks household-name status.

c4.evidence: Management repeatedly stresses making cancer medicines 'more accessible to patients worldwide' and reinvests heavily ($2.1B R&D in FY2025), but there is no single well-known published mission statement.

c6.evidence: “Chinese biotech, fast-growing, BRUKINSA, geopolitical risk” — investors see an impressive commercial success, though China ties and the BeiGene name change colour perception; overall mostly positive.

c7.evidence: Global oncology spending is a large, growing market driven by ageing populations, and BeOne guides 2026 revenue to $6.6-6.8B, up ~25% from $5.34B.

c8.evidence: It is expanding from blood cancers into solid tumours (CDK4 inhibitor in Phase 3 breast cancer, B7-H4 ADC, PD-1 combinations) and new modalities like the BTK degrader.

m1.evidence: Oyler set out in 2010 to build a global oncology company out of China using in-house clinical development, a vision now realised with most sales in the US.

m2.evidence: As co-founder and CEO for 16 years, Oyler has kept a long-term R&D-first strategy through years of multi-billion-dollar losses before reaching profitability in 2025.

m4.evidence: There is little independent evidence on Oyler's servant-leadership style beyond the company's stated 'Patients First' value.

m5.evidence: BeOne built an internal research engine (1,200+ scientists) that produced BRUKINSA, TEVIMBRA, sonrotoclax and the BGB-16673 degrader in-house.

m6.evidence: Oyler is a business founder (MIT undergraduate, Stanford MBA) rather than a scientist; scientific leadership comes from co-founder Xiaodong Wang and the R&D team.

m7.evidence: The company's founding goal of affordable, accessible cancer drugs suggests purpose beyond profit, though there is no strong independent evidence either way.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Oyler giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Oyler keeps a relatively low public profile and is not a celebrity CEO.

m9.evidence: Under Oyler revenue rose from $309M in FY2020 to $5.34B in FY2025 and the company turned a $447M GAAP operating profit in FY2025 after years of losses.

m10.evidence: Its cost-efficient in-house clinical model is a strategic frugality, but opex of $4.2B in FY2025 and big new plants (e.g. $800M+ Hopewell, NJ, plus a $300M expansion) are not frugal in absolute terms.

c10.evidence: Its medicines have treated about 2 million patients across 40+ markets, meaningful for cancer patients though far smaller in reach than consumer platforms.

p2.evidence: Discovering and getting approved first-in-class or best-in-class cancer drugs is extremely hard and important; BeOne has done it repeatedly from its own labs.

f2.evidence: Product gross margin improved from about 77% in FY2020 to 87.3% in FY2025, and operating margin swung from deeply negative to +8.4% in FY2025.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it held $5.10B cash and equivalents against $1.07B of debt, with shareholders' equity of $5.17B.

f4.evidence: Operating income improved from a $1.66B loss in FY2020 to $447M profit in FY2025, and operating cash flow turned from -$1.16B (FY2023) to +$1.13B (FY2025).

v1.evidence: In CLL, BRUKINSA is the only BTK inhibitor to beat ibrutinib head-to-head on efficacy with fewer heart problems, a simple reason to choose it, though Calquence and Jaypirca remain credible alternatives.

v2.evidence: BeOne does not appear on major best-places-to-work rankings such as Fortune 100 Best Companies; employee sentiment data is limited.

c5.evidence: Thousands of CLL, lymphoma and gastric/esophageal cancer patients on BRUKINSA and TEVIMBRA, and their oncologists, would miss a best-in-class, well-tolerated therapy if it disappeared.
